claim: Positive-strand RNA viruses represent the largest genetic class of viruses.
source: Positive-strand RNA viruses, whose virions contain mRNA-sense single stranded RNA, represent the largest genetic class of viruses (King et al., 2012), including many human, animal, and plant pathogens.
evidence: Supported by citation to King et al., 2012

claim: Positive-strand RNA viruses include numerous important pathogens such as Zika virus.
source: Positive-strand RNA viruses, the largest genetic class of viruses, include numerous important pathogens such as Zika virus.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: Positive-strand RNA viruses replicate their RNA genomes in membrane-bounded mini-organelles.
source: These viruses replicate their RNA genomes in novel, membrane-bounded mini-organelles, but the organization of viral proteins and RNAs in these compartments has been largely unknown.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: FHV RNA replication compartments are spherular invaginations of outer mitochondrial membranes.
source: These spherular invaginations of outer mitochondrial membranes are packed with electron-dense RNA fibrils and their volumes are closely correlated with RNA replication template length.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data presented in the study

claim: FHV spherules are packed with electron-dense RNA fibrils.
source: These spherular invaginations of outer mitochondrial membranes are packed with electron-dense RNA fibrils and their volumes are closely correlated with RNA replication template length.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Videos 2-3

claim: FHV spherule volumes are closely correlated with RNA replication template length.
source: These spherular invaginations of outer mitochondrial membranes are packed with electron-dense RNA fibrils and their volumes are closely correlated with RNA replication template length.
evidence: Supported by measurements of 1592 spherules shown in Figure 4

claim: Each FHV spherule's necked aperture is crowned by a cupped ring structure containing protein A.
source: Each spherule's necked aperture is crowned by a striking cupped ring structure containing multifunctional FHV RNA replication protein A.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data in Figures 5-6 and immunogold labeling in Figure 7

claim: FHV crowns exhibit twelve-fold symmetry.
source: Subtomogram averaging of these crowns revealed twelve-fold symmetry, concentric flanking protrusions, and a central electron density.
evidence: Supported by subtomogram averaging data shown in Figure 6, including power spectrum analysis showing peak at rotational Fourier component 12

claim: FHV crowns have concentric flanking protrusions.
source: Subtomogram averaging of these crowns revealed twelve-fold symmetry, concentric flanking protrusions, and a central electron density.
evidence: Supported by subtomogram averaging data shown in Figure 6

claim: FHV crowns have a central electron density.
source: Subtomogram averaging of these crowns revealed twelve-fold symmetry, concentric flanking protrusions, and a central electron density.
evidence: Supported by subtomogram averaging data shown in Figure 6

claim: Many FHV crowns were associated with long cytoplasmic fibrils, likely to be exported progeny RNA.
source: Many crowns were associated with long cytoplasmic fibrils, likely to be exported progeny RNA.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography observations in Figure 5 and Videos 1-3, with interpretation based on known function

claim: Positive-strand RNA viruses complete their entire replication cycle in the host cell cytoplasm.
source: These viruses complete their entire replication cycle in the host cell cytoplasm.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Positive-strand RNA viruses expand and rearrange host cellular membranes to generate sites for genomic RNA replication.
source: To generate sites for their genomic RNA replication, positive-strand RNA viruses expand and rearrange host cellular membranes (Fernández de Castro et al., 2017; den Boon et al., 2010; Kovalev et al., 2016; Paul and Bartenschlager, 2013; Paul et al., 2014; Romero-Brey and Bartenschlager, 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Membrane-associated RNA replication sites concentrate essential viral and host factors.
source: Such membrane-associated RNA replication sites are thought to concentrate essential viral and host factors, and to organize successive steps for efficient viral RNA synthesis (Atasheva et al., 2010; Neuvonen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Atasheva et al., 2010 and Neuvonen et al., 2011

claim: Membrane-associated RNA replication sites organize successive steps for efficient viral RNA synthesis.
source: Such membrane-associated RNA replication sites are thought to concentrate essential viral and host factors, and to organize successive steps for efficient viral RNA synthesis (Atasheva et al., 2010; Neuvonen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Atasheva et al., 2010 and Neuvonen et al., 2011

claim: Membrane-associated replication sites might provide protection from cellular nucleases.
source: Depending on their architecture and topology, such sites also might provide some protection from cellular nucleases and recognition by antiviral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) sensors, such as RIG-I, MDA-5, and AGO (Ahmad and Hur, 2015; Andrejeva et al., 2004; Diao et al., 2007; Fagard et al., 2000; van Rij et al., 2006; Weinmann et al., 2009; Yoneyama et al., 2004)
evidence: Presented as speculation supported by multiple citations

claim: Membrane-associated replication sites might provide protection from recognition by antiviral dsRNA sensors such as RIG-I, MDA-5, and AGO.
source: Depending on their architecture and topology, such sites also might provide some protection from cellular nucleases and recognition by antiviral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) sensors, such as RIG-I, MDA-5, and AGO (Ahmad and Hur, 2015; Andrejeva et al., 2004; Diao et al., 2007; Fagard et al., 2000; van Rij et al., 2006; Weinmann et al., 2009; Yoneyama et al., 2004)
evidence: Presented as speculation supported by multiple citations

claim: Membrane-associated replication sites help spatially segregate the viral RNA genome's competing functions as mRNA, replication template, and encapsidation substrate.
source: and help to spatially segregate the viral RNA genome's competing functions as an mRNA for viral protein synthesis, a template for viral RNA synthesis, and a substrate for encapsidation.
evidence: Presented as inference based on known functions

claim: RNA replication on expanded, rearranged cellular membranes is universal among positive-strand RNA viruses.
source: RNA replication on expanded, rearranged cellular membranes is universal among positive-strand RNA viruses and thus presents a target for broadly applicable antiviral therapies.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The structural organization of viral RNAs and proteins at membrane-associated sites of RNA replication has been largely unknown.
source: The structural organization of viral RNAs and proteins at such membrane-associated sites of RNA replication has been largely unknown.
evidence: Stated as background knowledge gap

claim: The FHV genome comprises RNA1 and RNA2, encoding replicase protein A and capsid proteins, respectively.
source: The bi-partite genome comprises RNA1 and RNA2, encoding the viral replicase protein A and the viral capsid proteins, respectively (Venter and Schneemann, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Venter and Schneemann, 2008

claim: FHV RNA1 directs the synthesis of RNA3, a subgenomic mRNA encoding protein B2.
source: RNA1 further directs the synthesis of RNA3, a subgenomic mRNA encoding protein B2, which counters host RNA interference defenses (Chao et al., 2005; Li et al., 2002; Lingel et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chao et al., 2005; Li et al., 2002; Lingel et al., 2005

claim: FHV protein B2 counters host RNA interference defenses.
source: RNA1 further directs the synthesis of RNA3, a subgenomic mRNA encoding protein B2, which counters host RNA interference defenses (Chao et al., 2005; Li et al., 2002; Lingel et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chao et al., 2005; Li et al., 2002; Lingel et al., 2005

claim: FHV protein A has an N-terminal mitochondrial membrane association domain.
source: Figure 1B shows the organization of protein A functional domains, including an N-terminal mitochondrial membrane association domain (Miller and Ahlquist, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller and Ahlquist, 2002 and shown in Figure 1B

claim: FHV protein A contains an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase domain.
source: Figure 1B shows the organization of protein A functional domains, including an N-terminal mitochondrial membrane association domain (Miller and Ahlquist, 2002), an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase domain, an RNA capping domain
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and stated in text

claim: FHV protein A contains an RNA capping domain.
source: Figure 1B shows the organization of protein A functional domains, including an N-terminal mitochondrial membrane association domain (Miller and Ahlquist, 2002), an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase domain, an RNA capping domain
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and stated in text

claim: FHV protein A has multiple independent multimerization regions.
source: and multiple independent multimerization regions identified by fluorescence resonance energy transfer (Dye et al., 2005b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dye et al., 2005b

claim: FHV infection of Drosophila cells induces ~50 nm diameter spherule invaginations of outer mitochondrial membranes.
source: Previous transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and EM tomography by our group and others showed that FHV infection of Drosophila cells induces ~50 nm diameter 'spherule' invaginations of the outer mitochondrial membranes (Kopek et al., 2007; Lanman et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2001; Short et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: FHV spherules are the sites of viral protein A replicase accumulation and viral RNA synthesis.
source: These spherules are the sites of viral protein A replicase accumulation and viral RNA synthesis (Kopek et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kopek et al., 2007

claim: FHV spherules remain connected to the cytoplasm via a neck-like aperture.
source: and remain connected to the cytoplasm via a neck-like aperture (Kopek et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kopek et al., 2007 and Miller et al., 2001

claim: Similar spherule RNA replication compartments are formed by many positive-strand RNA viruses including flaviviruses and alphaviruses.
source: Similar spherule RNA replication compartments are formed on various intracellular membranes by many positive-strand RNA viruses, such as the human-infecting flaviviruses, alphaviruses, and many others (Belov et al., 2007, 2012; den Boon and Ahlquist, 2010; den Boon et al., 2010; Diaz et al., 2012, 2010; Knoops et al., 2012; Kopek et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2001; Schwartz et al., 2002; Welsch et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Chemical fixation and plastic embedding are prone to fixation-induced artifacts.
source: While informative, these older images were derived from FHV-infected and other virus-infected cells and cell fractions that were chemically fixed and embedded in plastic, which are prone to fixation-induced artifacts (McDonald and Auer, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to McDonald and Auer, 2006

claim: Heavy metal staining did not allow visualizing viral RNAs and replication proteins in spherules.
source: Moreover, these heavy metal stained samples defined the low-resolution ultrastructure of the bounding spherule membranes, but did not allow visualizing the viral RNAs and replication proteins.
evidence: Stated as limitation of prior methods

claim: Cryo-EM presents samples in a much more native state than chemical fixation.
source: Cryo-EM presents samples in a much more native state, bypasses heavy metal staining, and images the sample's intrinsic electron density, providing direct visualization of all components – lipid, RNA, and protein – of the RNA replication complexes (Bertin et al., 2012; Gold et al., 2014; Meyerson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bertin et al., 2012; Gold et al., 2014; Meyerson et al., 2011

claim: Cryo-EM bypasses heavy metal staining and images the sample's intrinsic electron density.
source: Cryo-EM presents samples in a much more native state, bypasses heavy metal staining, and images the sample's intrinsic electron density, providing direct visualization of all components – lipid, RNA, and protein – of the RNA replication complexes (Bertin et al., 2012; Gold et al., 2014; Meyerson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bertin et al., 2012; Gold et al., 2014; Meyerson et al., 2011

claim: Cryo-EM provides direct visualization of all components (lipid, RNA, and protein) of RNA replication complexes.
source: Cryo-EM presents samples in a much more native state, bypasses heavy metal staining, and images the sample's intrinsic electron density, providing direct visualization of all components – lipid, RNA, and protein – of the RNA replication complexes (Bertin et al., 2012; Gold et al., 2014; Meyerson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bertin et al., 2012; Gold et al., 2014; Meyerson et al., 2011

claim: Mitochondria isolated from FHV-infected Drosophila cells retain RNA replication compartments that are active in viral RNA synthesis.
source: Previously our group showed that mitochondria isolated from FHV-infected Drosophila cells retain RNA replication compartments (spherules) that are active in viral RNA synthesis with a specific activity approaching that in infected cells (Kopek et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kopek et al., 2007

claim: Mitochondria from mock-infected cells have closely appressed outer and inner mitochondrial membranes.
source: As expected, mitochondria from mock-infected cells had closely appressed outer and inner mitochondrial membranes, with inner membrane cristae extensions into the interior matrix (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM imaging shown in Figure 2A

claim: The outer and inner membranes of mitochondria from FHV-infected cells are separated.
source: By contrast, and consistent with previous reports (Kopek et al., 2007, 2010; Lanman et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2001; Short et al., 2016), the outer and inner membranes of mitochondria from FHV-infected cells were separated, and the intervening space filled with numerous membrane spherules.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM imaging shown in Figure 2B and citations to prior work

claim: The space between outer and inner membranes of FHV-infected mitochondria is filled with numerous membrane spherules.
source: By contrast, and consistent with previous reports (Kopek et al., 2007, 2010; Lanman et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2001; Short et al., 2016), the outer and inner membranes of mitochondria from FHV-infected cells were separated, and the intervening space filled with numerous membrane spherules.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM imaging shown in Figure 2B and citations to prior work

claim: In chemically-fixed samples, FHV RNA replication complexes had oblong shapes significantly elongated perpendicular to the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: While, in chemically-fixed samples, FHV RNA replication complexes had oblong shapes significantly elongated perpendicular to the outer mitochondrial membrane (Kopek et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2001), in plunge-frozen samples they were much more spherical (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kopek et al., 2007 and Miller et al., 2001

claim: In plunge-frozen samples, FHV RNA replication complexes are much more spherical than in chemically-fixed samples.
source: While, in chemically-fixed samples, FHV RNA replication complexes had oblong shapes significantly elongated perpendicular to the outer mitochondrial membrane (Kopek et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2001), in plunge-frozen samples they were much more spherical (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM imaging shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mitochondria isolated from FHV-infected cells are highly active in viral RNA synthesis.
source: As in our prior studies (Kopek et al., 2007), we confirmed that mitochondria isolated from FHV-infected cells retained the biological integrity of the spherules that were highly active in viral RNA synthesis (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by RNA synthesis assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Rapid cryo-fixation improved preservation of FHV replication compartments.
source: As expected, rapid cryo-fixation improved preservation and direct imaging of the native electron density of these samples greatly facilitated visualizing non-membrane components of these replication compartments, including RNAs and protein structures, at much higher resolution and revealing multiple striking features.
evidence: Based on comparison of cryo-EM results with prior chemical fixation results

claim: Cryo-EM revealed a wider range of spherule diameters than previously observed.
source: These included a wider range of spherule diameters than previously observed, coiled interior filaments filling the invaginated membrane vesicle, an ~25–30 nm diameter by 20 nm-high cupped density crowning the cytoplasmic side of each spherule neck, and usually single exterior filaments extending from these crown structures into the extra-mitochondrial cytoplasmic space (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data shown in Videos 1 and 2

claim: Coiled interior filaments fill the invaginated membrane vesicle of FHV spherules.
source: These included a wider range of spherule diameters than previously observed, coiled interior filaments filling the invaginated membrane vesicle, an ~25–30 nm diameter by 20 nm-high cupped density crowning the cytoplasmic side of each spherule neck, and usually single exterior filaments extending from these crown structures into the extra-mitochondrial cytoplasmic space (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data shown in Videos 1 and 2

claim: An ~25–30 nm diameter by 20 nm-high cupped density crowns the cytoplasmic side of each spherule neck.
source: These included a wider range of spherule diameters than previously observed, coiled interior filaments filling the invaginated membrane vesicle, an ~25–30 nm diameter by 20 nm-high cupped density crowning the cytoplasmic side of each spherule neck, and usually single exterior filaments extending from these crown structures into the extra-mitochondrial cytoplasmic space (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data shown in Videos 1 and 2

claim: Usually single exterior filaments extend from crown structures into the extra-mitochondrial cytoplasmic space.
source: These included a wider range of spherule diameters than previously observed, coiled interior filaments filling the invaginated membrane vesicle, an ~25–30 nm diameter by 20 nm-high cupped density crowning the cytoplasmic side of each spherule neck, and usually single exterior filaments extending from these crown structures into the extra-mitochondrial cytoplasmic space (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data shown in Videos 1 and 2

claim: FHV spherule interiors are densely packed with filaments that appear as closely packed rods in cross-section.
source: In keeping with this, our new cryo-EM imaging revealed FHV spherule interiors to be densely packed with filaments that appeared in cross-section as closely packed rods and in side views as long strands curved within the spherules (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Many of the filament segments visualized in individual cross-sections are connected between successive tomographic slices.
source: Videos 2 and 3 provide continuous views through the complete volume of numerous spherules, showing that many of the filament segments visualized in individual cross-sections are connected between successive tomographic slices.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data shown in Videos 2 and 3

claim: The curved filaments in FHV spherules occupy essentially the full spherule interior in a pattern reminiscent of a ball of yarn.
source: Highlighting this interior electron density with a computed tomography software package (AMIRA, FEI) provided three-dimensional views, further illustrating that these curved filaments occupy essentially the full spherule interior in a pattern reminiscent of a ball of yarn (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: Individual sectioned views frequently displayed continuous, relatively straight filament segments at least 40 nm long.
source: While the current tomographic resolution did not allow unambiguous tracing of the full length of these filaments, individual sectioned views such as in Figure 3D frequently displayed continuous, relatively straight segments at least 40 nm long, consistent with estimates of ~60–64 nm for the persistence length of dsRNA, i.e. the length of dsRNA required to show significant bending (Abels, Moreno-Herrero, Abels et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The persistence length of dsRNA is ~60–64 nm.
source: consistent with estimates of ~60–64 nm for the persistence length of dsRNA, i.e. the length of dsRNA required to show significant bending (Abels, Moreno-Herrero, Abels et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abels, Moreno-Herrero, Abels et al., 2005

claim: 1592 spherules were measured from four reconstructed tomograms across four independent experiments.
source: To explore this distribution of spherule sizes more precisely, we measured the volume of 1592 spherules from four reconstructed tomograms derived from FHV-infected cells across four independent experiments.
evidence: Stated as experimental method

claim: The average spherule diameter is ~50 nm.
source: The average spherule diameter was ~50 nm, consistent with prior observations (Kopek et al., 2007, 2010; Miller et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by measurements of 1592 spherules and citations to prior work

claim: The range of spherule diameters varies from ~30 to nearly 70 nm.
source: but the range of spherule diameters varied from ~30 to nearly 70 nm.
evidence: Supported by measurements of 1592 spherules

claim: The spherule volume range is between 13,600 nm³ and 145,500 nm³.
source: The corresponding volume range was between 13,600 nm3 and 145,500 nm3, with an average spherule volume of 66,100 nm3 and a standard deviation of ±32,900 nm3.
evidence: Calculated from measurements of 1592 spherules

claim: The average spherule volume is 66,100 nm³ with a standard deviation of ±32,900 nm³.
source: The corresponding volume range was between 13,600 nm3 and 145,500 nm3, with an average spherule volume of 66,100 nm3 and a standard deviation of ±32,900 nm3.
evidence: Calculated from measurements of 1592 spherules

claim: The distribution of spherule volumes shows three to four peaks.
source: When plotted, the distribution of spherule volumes showed three to four peaks, suggesting the possibility of distinct size classes of spherules (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A

claim: All FHV spherules observed in cryo-EM experiments contained interior filaments at similar packing density.
source: All FHV spherules observed in these cryo-EM experiments contained interior filaments at similar packing density (Figure 3 and Video 3)
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography observations shown in Figure 3 and Video 3

claim: Spherules of varying diameter must contain varying amounts of RNA.
source: All FHV spherules observed in these cryo-EM experiments contained interior filaments at similar packing density (Figure 3 and Video 3), implying that spherules of varying diameter must contain varying amounts of RNA.
evidence: Inferred from observation of similar packing density across different spherule sizes

claim: The presence of multiple spherule size classes in full FHV infection might be related to the replication of three viral RNA templates (RNA1, RNA2, and RNA3) occurring in different spherules.
source: Thus, the presence of multiple spherule size classes in full FHV infection might be related to the replication of three viral RNA templates, genomic RNA1 and RNA2, and subgenomic (sg) RNA3, with respective lengths of 3.1, 1.4, and 0.4 kb, occurring in different spherules.
evidence: Presented as speculation based on observed size distribution

claim: Cells expressing protein A and RNA1 template produce two distinct spherule size populations.
source: Figure 4B shows the results for cells expressing protein A and an FHV genomic RNA1 template: volumes measured for 541 spherules from three tomograms from two independent transfection experiments revealed that this combination produced two distinct spherule size populations reflecting the extremes of the distribution produced by full FHV infection
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 4B

claim: RNA1 replication gives rise to 3.1 kb RNA1 and 0.4 kb sgRNA3 progeny.
source: consistent with the fact that RNA1 replication gives rise to 3.1 kb RNA1 and 0.4 kb sgRNA3 progeny.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The larger spherule class from RNA1 replication distributes around a volume of ~108,000 nm³.
source: The larger spherule class distributed around a volume of ~108,000 nm3, the smaller spherule class around ~12,000 nm3.
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 4B

claim: The smaller spherule class from RNA1 replication distributes around ~12,000 nm³.
source: The larger spherule class distributed around a volume of ~108,000 nm3, the smaller spherule class around ~12,000 nm3.
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 4B

claim: Cells expressing protein A and sgRNA3 template produce spherule volumes closely matching the smaller size class of spherules induced by RNA1 and RNA3 replication.
source: Similarly, Figure 4C shows the results for cells expressing protein A and an FHV sgRNA3 template: the resulting spherules volumes closely matching the smaller size class of spherules induced by simultaneous replication of RNA1 and RNA3.
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 4C

claim: The size distribution of FHV RNA replication compartments is strongly correlated with the length of the viral RNA template being replicated.
source: Thus, the size distribution of FHV RNA replication compartments is strongly correlated with the length of the viral RNA template or templates being replicated.
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 4

claim: RNA2 replication requires trans-activation by RNA3.
source: RNA2 replication requires trans-activation by RNA3 (Lindenbach et al., 2002; Eckerle and Ball, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lindenbach et al., 2002 and Eckerle and Ball, 2002

claim: Some spherules might contain both RNA2 and RNA3.
source: which could lead to some spherules containing both RNA2 and RNA3.
evidence: Presented as speculation based on trans-activation requirement

claim: The size and RNA content of individual spherules might vary dynamically through ongoing processes of RNA synthesis and RNA export.
source: Moreover, through ongoing processes of RNA synthesis and RNA export, the size and RNA content of individual spherules might vary dynamically.
evidence: Presented as speculation

claim: The filaments in FHV spherules are likely dsRNA.
source: To more precisely address the relationship between FHV RNA template length and spherule volume, we further considered packaging density under the assumption that the filaments in FHV spherules are dsRNA, which as noted above appears likely from biochemical and other data.
evidence: Based on inference from biochemical data and structural similarity

claim: The filaments and their arrangement in FHV spherules are generally similar to those of dsRNA templates in the replicative cores of dsRNA viruses.
source: The filaments and their arrangement in concentric, wound layers were generally similar to those of dsRNA templates in the replicative cores of dsRNA viruses (Figure 3, Video 1)
evidence: Based on comparison with known structures shown in Figure 3 and Video 1

claim: The average inter-filament distance in CPV is 2.7 nm.
source: For CPV and FHV the average inter-filament distances are 2.7 nm (Zhang et al., 2015) and 6.4 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015

claim: The average inter-filament distance in FHV spherules is 6.4 nm.
source: For CPV and FHV the average inter-filament distances are 2.7 nm (Zhang et al., 2015) and 6.4 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), respectively.
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The dsRNA packing density in FHV spherules is ~5.8 fold lower than CPV's 334 bp / 1000 nm³.
source: Thus, the dsRNA packing density in FHV spherules should be ~5.8 fold lower than CPV's 334 bp / 1000 nm3 (~24.7 kbp dsRNA genome per ~74,000 nm3 [Cheng et al., 2011]).
evidence: Calculated from inter-filament distance measurements and CPV reference data

claim: At a calculated density of ~58 bp / 1000 nm³, dsRNA1 (3.1 kbp) would occupy ~53,000 nm³.
source: At a resulting calculated density of ~58 bp / 1000 nm3, dsRNA1 (3.1 kbp), dsRNA2 (1.4 kbp), and dsRNA3 (0.4 kbp) would occupy ~53,000 nm3, ~24,000 nm3, and ~7000 nm3, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from packing density estimate

claim: At a calculated density of ~58 bp / 1000 nm³, dsRNA2 (1.4 kbp) would occupy ~24,000 nm³.
source: At a resulting calculated density of ~58 bp / 1000 nm3, dsRNA1 (3.1 kbp), dsRNA2 (1.4 kbp), and dsRNA3 (0.4 kbp) would occupy ~53,000 nm3, ~24,000 nm3, and ~7000 nm3, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from packing density estimate

claim: At a calculated density of ~58 bp / 1000 nm³, dsRNA3 (0.4 kbp) would occupy ~7000 nm³.
source: At a resulting calculated density of ~58 bp / 1000 nm3, dsRNA1 (3.1 kbp), dsRNA2 (1.4 kbp), and dsRNA3 (0.4 kbp) would occupy ~53,000 nm3, ~24,000 nm3, and ~7000 nm3, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from packing density estimate

claim: Even the smallest RNA1-associated spherules could accommodate a complete RNA1 dsRNA.
source: Accordingly, even the smallest of the RNA1-associated ~80,000–130,000 nm3 spherules (Figure 4B) could accommodate a complete RNA1 dsRNA, consistent with the need for at least one negative-strand template to support positive-strand synthesis
evidence: Based on comparison of calculated RNA volume with measured spherule volumes

claim: Similar levels of negative- and positive-strand FHV RNAs fractionate from infected cells in a mitochondrially-associated, nuclease-protected state.
source: and our finding for each of FHV RNAs 1, 2 and 3 that similar levels of negative- and positive-strand fractionate from infected cells in a mitochondrially-associated, nuclease-protected state (N. Unchwaniwala and P. Ahlquist, unpublished results).
evidence: Stated as unpublished data from the authors

claim: Even the smallest RNA3-associated spherules could accommodate a complete RNA3 dsRNA.
source: Similarly, even the smallest of the RNA3-associated ~7,000–15,000 nm3 spherules (Figure 4B and C) could accommodate a complete RNA3 dsRNA.
evidence: Based on comparison of calculated RNA volume with measured spherule volumes

claim: Previous examination of chemically-fixed FHV replication compartments revealed electron-dense structures on the cytoplasmic surface of outer mitochondrial membranes immediately above spherule necks.
source: Our previous examination of chemically-fixed, plastic-embedded samples of FHV replication compartments in whole infected cells, using both two-dimensional transmission EM imaging (Kopek et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2001) and three-dimensional tomographic reconstruction (Kopek et al., 2007), had revealed the regular presence of electron-dense structures on the cytoplasmic surface of outer mitochondrial membranes immediately above the necks of FHV spherules.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: In top views, crown structures appear circular with a small central electron density.
source: In top views perpendicular to the mitochondrial surface these structure appeared circular, with a small central electron density (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Top views of crowns reveal an outer concentric ring of regularly spaced small densities.
source: In many cases, close inspection of such top views revealed an outer concentric ring of regularly spaced small densities (Figure 5B inset, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM tomography data shown in Figure 5B inset and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Subtomogram averaging was performed on regions surrounding the apertures of over 300 individual spherules.
source: To better visualize these striking new features, we performed iterative subtomogram averaging (Castaño-Díez et al., 2012) of the regions surrounding the apertures of over 300 individual spherules
evidence: Stated as experimental method

claim: The subtomogram-averaged reconstruction of the spherule aperture structure has a resolution estimated at approximately 3.3 nm.
source: and reconstructed a three-dimensional image with a resolution estimated at approximately 3.3 nm (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and Video 4).
evidence: Supported by Fourier shell correlation analysis shown in Figure 6G

claim: Power spectrum calculations showed a strong peak at rotational Fourier component 12.
source: While no symmetry was artificially imposed, power spectrum calculations showed a strong peak at rotational Fourier component 12 (Figure 6H)
evidence: Supported by power spectrum analysis shown in Figure 6H

claim: The averaged reconstruction of the spherule aperture structure revealed a clear twelve-fold symmetry.
source: and accordingly, the averaged reconstruction of the spherule aperture structure revealed a clear twelve-fold symmetry.
evidence: Supported by subtomogram averaging shown in Figure 6

claim: The crown structure has a central ~19 nm diameter turret projection.
source: The reconstructed structure showed a central ~19 nm diameter 'turret' projection, surrounded by an outer, ~35 nm diameter ring of twelve smaller 'teeth' (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by subtomogram averaging shown in Figure 6

claim: The crown structure has an outer ~35 nm diameter ring of twelve smaller teeth.
source: The reconstructed structure showed a central ~19 nm diameter 'turret' projection, surrounded by an outer, ~35 nm diameter ring of twelve smaller 'teeth' (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by subtomogram averaging shown in Figure 6

claim: The twelve teeth are spaced ~4 nm apart.
source: spaced ~4 nm apart, projected ~3 nm above the outer membrane surface, and angled slightly toward the turret (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: Supported by subtomogram averaging shown in Figure 6C-F

claim: The twelve teeth project ~3 nm above the outer membrane surface.
source: spaced ~4 nm apart, projected ~3 nm above the outer membrane surface, and angled slightly toward the turret (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: Supported by subtomogram averaging shown in Figure 6C-F

claim: The twelve teeth are angled slightly toward the turret.

claim: At its highest dimension, the turret is raised ~14 nm above the outer mitochondrial membrane surface.

claim: The turret resides in a slight depression of the outer mitochondrial membrane.

evidence: Supported by subtomogram averaging shown in Figure 6A and E

claim: Within the turret, a central ~11 nm diameter open channel into the spherule is present.

evidence: Supported by subtomogram averaging and citations to prior work

claim: A strongly averaged central density within the turret is consistent with filamentous extrusions observed in the original tomograms.

evidence: Based on comparison of subtomogram average with original tomograms

claim: The central density within the turret must have been present in the majority of crown densities used for subtomogram averaging.

evidence: Inferred from retention of density in averaged reconstruction

claim: Crown structures are present on FHV spherules but absent on mitochondria from mock-infected cells.

evidence: Supported by comparison of infected and mock-infected samples shown in Video 5

claim: Crown structures either consist of or are induced by viral factors.
source: The presence of crown structures on FHV spherules and their absence on mitochondria from mock-infected cells (Video 5) indicated that they either consist of or are induced by viral factors.
evidence: Inferred from presence in infected cells and absence in mock-infected cells

claim: FHV protein A is the sole FHV protein required for RNA replication.
source: First, protein A, having RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, RNA capping, and other functions, is the sole FHV protein required for RNA replication (Dye et al., 2005a; Miller and Ahlquist, 2002; Miller et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dye et al., 2005a; Miller and Ahlquist, 2002; Miller et al., 2003

claim: Protein A localizes to outer mitochondrial membranes via an N-terminal trans-membrane segment.
source: Protein A localizes to outer mitochondrial membranes via an N-terminal trans-membrane segment (Miller and Ahlquist, 2002; Miller et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Miller and Ahlquist, 2002 and Miller et al., 2003

claim: Protein A self-interacts through multiple domains in ways critical for RNA replication.

evidence: Supported by citation to Dye et al., 2005b

claim: Anti-protein A immunogold labeling produced abundant gold labeling on the cytoplasmic side of outer mitochondrial membranes only above membrane regions where spherules were present.

claim: Negative controls with regular rabbit IgG antibodies did not show significant immuno-gold labeling.

evidence: Supported by negative control data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The high density of anti-protein A gold particles in the vicinity of each spherule is potentially consistent with the 12-fold symmetry of crowns.

evidence: Based on comparison of immunogold labeling density with crown symmetry

claim: The dense clustering of protein A-targeted immunogold labeling strictly above spherules strongly indicates that protein A is a major component of the FHV crown structure.
source: Thus, the dense clustering of protein A-targeted immunogold labeling strictly above spherules strongly indicates that protein A is a major component of the FHV crown structure.
evidence: Based on immunogold labeling data shown in Figure 7

claim: When imaged by EM and electron tomography of chemically fixed samples, spherules appeared elongated parallel to the neck axis and with indistinct contents.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Rapid cryo-fixation uniformly revealed nearly round spherules that were densely packed with internal filaments.

claim: The internal filaments in FHV spherules strongly resemble genomic dsRNAs in reovirus virions.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

source: or that export of progeny positive-strand RNAs may not be coincident with their synthesis.

source: The correlation between spherule volume and RNA template size might be a more general property of positive-strand RNA virus replication.

source: For example, the alphavirus Semliki forest virus (SFV), which replicates its genome in similar spherular replication compartments on the plasma membrane, also shows a correlation of spherule size and template length (Kallio et al., 2013).

claim: The crown volume is sufficient to encompass 12 copies of protein A.
source: Moreover, calculations based on the average density of globular proteins show that the crown volume is sufficient to encompass 12 copies of protein A.

source: In addition, while these findings show that protein A is a major component of the crown, present results do not rule out that other viral or host proteins might also be recruited into the crown along with protein A.

claim: The crown plays a major role in stabilizing the high-energy spherule membrane deformation.
source: The crown's prominent position ringing the necked spherule aperture, its extensive engagement with the mitochondrial outer membrane, its 12-fold symmetry, and its dense labeling by antibodies against trans-membrane FHV protein A all imply that the crown plays a major role in stabilizing the high-energy spherule membrane deformation.
evidence: Inferred from structural features and protein composition

claim: Herpes simplex virus has 12-mer viral protein rings as DNA packaging portal complexes.

evidence: Supported by citations to Simpson et al., 2000 and Lhuillier et al., 2009

claim: dsRNA Cystoviridae encode a hexameric portal protein ring that translocates parental RNA genome templates into virions and releases nascent viral RNA products to the cytoplasm.

claim: Prior immunogold labeling of sectioned mitochondria revealed that some protein A resides within spherules.

source: Localization to more than one site, possibly in alternate multimeric forms (Dye et al., 2005a), could be related to protein A's many roles in spherule formation, negative- and positive-strand genomic RNA synthesis, sgRNA3 synthesis, and RNA capping (Ball, 1995; Eckerle et al., 2003; Johnson and Ball, 1999; Kopek et al., 2010; Lindenbach et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: Presented as speculation supported by citations

claim: Protein A recruits FHV genomic RNA to mitochondrial membranes through specific cis-acting RNA signals in a step separable from later RNA synthesis and spherule formation.

claim: The spherule may be formed by injecting the nascent RNA product of negative-strand RNA synthesis onto the cytoplasmic side of the mitochondrial membrane, causing its deformation and invagination.
source: Specifically, the dependence on viral RNA synthesis, the densely filament-packed state of spherules (Videos 1 and 3), and the scaling of spherule size with RNA template length over a ≥10 fold range (Figure 4), all would be explained if the spherule was formed by injecting the nascent RNA product of negative-strand RNA synthesis onto the cytoplasmic side on the mitochondrial membrane, causing its deformation and invagination (Figure 8C).

claim: The FHV crown could provide a highly stable platform to drive genome translocation and the associated lipid flow required to expand the growing spherule vesicle.

evidence: Presented as speculation

claim: Single RNA polymerases generate forces of ~25 pN.
